## Overview

We conducted a resource selection function (RSF) based on 718 known active lek
locations throughout the state of Nevada to 1) predict areas with potential
lekking activity and 2) quantify active lek site characteristics. We used a
use-availability study design where each lek site was considered a sampling
unit. Leks were the "used" points in the analysis and were compared to
randomly generated "available" points. This document reports the current
(v4) analysis, produced by a fully scripted pipeline in which every input is
fetched from its authoritative public source, every intermediate is staged as
GeoParquet or Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFF, and every run is reproducible from a
cold start. **No lek locations appear in this document or in any public
artifact of this project.**

## Study Area

![Study area: the sage-grouse distribution range in Nevada (USFWS 2015 Status
Review current range), with 5-km buffers around active leks falling outside
the range.](v4/figs/study_area.png){width=55%}

We determined the extent of the study — **152,458 km²** — using the
sage-grouse species distribution range for the state of Nevada, USA, combined
with a 5-km buffer around active leks that fell outside the traditional
range. Sage-grouse inhabit rangelands throughout the state generally
characterized as high-elevation, cool desert ecosystems with hot, dry summers
and cold winters. Wyoming big sagebrush (*Artemisia tridentata
wyomingensis*), low sagebrush (*A. arbuscula*), and black sagebrush
(*A. nova*) largely dominate areas below 2,100 m in elevation; at higher
elevations, mountain big sagebrush (*A. t. vaseyana*) is the dominant
vegetation. The dominant conifers include Utah juniper (*Juniperus
osteosperma*) and single-leaf pinyon pine (*Pinus monophylla*), which tend to
colonize mid- to high-elevation and mesic sagebrush habitats.

## Data Acquisition

Lek locations come from the state of Nevada's historical lek count dataset,
acquired from the Nevada Department of Wildlife (NDOW) in 2020. The dataset
includes lek center locations and annual male counts for all known leks
throughout Nevada from 1947–2018, with sites characterized as active,
inactive, historic, no activity, or unknown. This analysis uses leks
categorized as **active as of 2018** and located within Nevada (n = 718),
omitting all others. Lek data are held under agreement and are not
redistributed; researchers may request them from NDOW.

| Input | Source & product | Vintage | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lek locations | NDOW historical lek count dataset | counts 1947–2018 | acquired 2020, under agreement |
| Elevation | USGS 3DEP, 1 arc-second (30 m), 72 tiles | tile vintages 2013–2026 | TNM API, 2026-08-11, manifested |
| Vegetation | LANDFIRE LF2025 Existing Vegetation Type (EVT_PHYS) | LF2025 | LFPS API, 2026-08-11 |
| Roads | U.S. Census TIGER/Line, Nevada primary & secondary roads | 2024 | 2026-08-11 |
| Range polygon | USFWS 2015 Status Review current range | 2015 | ScienceBase API, 2026-08-11 |

All acquisition is performed by pipeline scripts that write provenance
manifests (exact URLs, publication dates, sizes) alongside the data. Note one
departure from earlier drafts: the roads layer is TIGER primary and secondary
roads; the 2024 draft's roads data additionally included minor and unimproved
roads. Road proximity did not enter the top model set in either analysis.

## Statistical Analysis

### Design

To ensure a sufficient number of random points to characterize availability
across the study area, we generated **7,180 random points — ten per used
lek** — as a seeded uniform sample within the study area (seed 20260811),
making the draw exactly reproducible. Each used and available site was
attributed with the full predictor set.

### Predictor variables

Environmental data included LANDFIRE Existing Vegetation Type physiognomy
(EVT_PHYS) and elevation from a 30-m digital elevation model. The vegetation
layer's categories — conifer, conifer-hardwood, exotic herbaceous, exotic
tree-shrub, grassland, quarries–strip mines–gravel pits–well/wind pads,
riparian, shrubland, sparsely vegetated, and other — follow the draft
analysis, with classes rarer than 10 sites collapsed into "other." DEM
derivatives included aspect, slope, curvature, and ruggedness. We categorized
aspect into eight cardinal directions (N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW).
Anthropogenic activity is represented by the Euclidean distance from each
site to the nearest road.

Ruggedness is the **Vector Ruggedness Measure** (VRM; Sappington et al.
2007), computed over a 3×3 (90 m × 90 m) window from the slope and aspect
surfaces: the dispersion of surface-normal vectors, a geometric property of
terrain. In developing v4 we evaluated range-position focal indices of the
form (mean − min)/(max − min) and found them dominated by DEM-generation-
specific texture — cells classified as "rugged" agreed only 63% of the time
across DEM vintages (chance = 50%) — and nearly uncorrelated with terrain
geometry. VRM is the standard ruggedness measure in the wildlife-habitat
literature and is decorrelated from slope by construction (r = 0.40 in our
design; VIF ≤ 1.5).

![Terrain covariates at 30 m (EPSG:5070), read from the pipeline's
Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs.](v4/figs/terrain.png)

### Models

Continuous covariates were standardized (z-scaled). We fit the twelve a
priori binomial GLMs of the draft analysis — additive combinations of road
proximity, curvature, ruggedness, slope, aspect direction, elevation, and
vegetation — ranked them by AICc, checked multicollinearity with variance
inflation factors (all ≤ 1.5), and averaged the top three models to generate
coefficient estimates with 85% confidence intervals.

sites.](v4/figs/distributions.png)

The separation visible above previews every model result: used sites
concentrate at low slope, low VRM, and higher elevation relative to

sites.](v4/figs/veg_proportions.png)

![Pearson correlations among continuous predictors. Slope and elevation carry

](v4/figs/correlation.png){width=60%}

**Summary statistics.**

{{< include v4/tables/summary_stats.md >}}

**Availability-sample validation.** Following the draft's S1 approach, we
compared the mean of the study area's pixels for each continuous variable
(estimated by a dense 100,000-point Monte Carlo sample at full raster
resolution) against the available-sample mean and its 85% CI:

{{< include v4/tables/validation.md >}}

The VRM interval misses the study-area mean by ~1% — a consequence of the
tight CI at n = 7,180 rather than a biased draw; elevation, slope, and
curvature are covered.

## Results

**Model selection** (all twelve a priori models, matching the draft's Table
3). The same three models lead the AICc ranking as in the draft analysis
(m1, m7, m2), in slightly different order:

{{< include v4/tables/model_selection.md >}}

**Model-averaged coefficients** (top three models, 85% CIs):

{{< include v4/tables/coefficients.md >}}

![Model-averaged terrain effects: 2024 draft versus v4. Note the ruggedness
instrument differs between analyses (draft: range-position focal index; v4:
VRM).](v4/figs/betas.png)

Lek sites were more likely to occur at **higher elevations** (model-averaged
β = 0.96, 85% CI 0.87–1.05) and less likely to occur on **steeper slopes**
(β = −1.19, 85% CI −1.34 – −1.05), closely replicating the draft analysis
(elevation 0.78; slope −1.42) on entirely current data. Measured with VRM,
lek sites show **strong avoidance of rugged terrain** (β = −1.02, 85% CI
−1.27 – −0.76): used sites average VRM 0.00046 against 0.00197 across
availability — display grounds sit on terrain roughly four times smoother
than the landscape offers.

**Model diagnostics.** Discrimination and out-of-sample stability were
assessed with the area under the ROC curve: **AUC = 0.801** for the full
model average, and **0.791 ± 0.012** under 5-fold cross-validation of the top
model — good discrimination that holds out of sample. Calibration by decile
of predicted probability tracks the identity line:

![Calibration: mean predicted probability versus observed use rate, by
decile.](v4/figs/calibration.png){width=48%}

Spatially blocked cross-validation and a Boyce index computed against the
full prediction surface are planned once the statewide prediction raster is
generated; reviewer history on this team's prior RSF work (Baum et al. 2022,
*Rangeland Ecology & Management* 84:117–125) indicates spatial structure will
be a review focus, and lek clustering will be addressed directly.

![Vegetation selection relative to the shrubland
reference.](v4/figs/vegetation.png)

Relative to shrubland, grassland and exotic herbaceous classes sit above the
reference while conifer, sparsely vegetated, and riparian classes fall well
below, with conifer most strongly avoided — consistent with the conifer-
encroachment literature and with the draft's vegetation ordering.

Together: leks occupy **gentle, smooth, relatively high, open ground** —
low slope, low surface ruggedness, higher elevation, herbaceous cover over
conifer. Each element of that description carries a coefficient with a clean
confidence interval, estimated against NDOW's lek register from current
public terrain and vegetation data.

## Reproducibility

```bash
uv run pipeline/fetch_vectors.py
python3 pipeline/fetch_tnm.py --dataset "National Elevation Dataset (NED) 1 arc-second" \
  --bbox="-120.01,35.0,-114.03,42.01" --manifest data/manifest-3dep-v4.json
bash pipeline/build_dem.sh
uv run pipeline/build_vrm.py
python3 pipeline/fetch_landfire.py --layer LF2025_EVT \
  --bbox "-120.01 35.0 -114.03 42.01" --email you@example.com \
  --out data-local/landfire/evt.zip
uv run pipeline/prepare_design.py
uv run pipeline/extract_covariates.py
Rscript pipeline/fit_models.R
uv run pipeline/render_figures.py && uv run pipeline/eda_figures.py
quarto render reports/findings.qmd
```

The design step is deterministic: rerunning it reproduces the design file
byte-for-byte. Lek data must be requested from NDOW. A container image and a
continuous-integration smoke test (small AOI) are planned so the chain runs
with one command on any machine.
